Ore Hauling Scheduling
Track SE-POMINTecnologias Inovadoras de Pesquisa Operacional na Mineração
LVIII Simpósio Brasileiro de Pesquisa Operacional · Belo Horizonte, MG · 2026

Scheduling-based optimization for open-pit ore hauling operations

The truck–loader assignment problem of a surface mine, formulated as parallel-machine scheduling with heterogeneous speeds and release times, and solved with an exact model, two constructive heuristics, a local search and two tabu-search metaheuristics.

Luis Tarazona-Torres  ·  Ciro Alberto Amaya  ·  David Álvarez-Martínez Department of Industrial Engineering · Universidad de los Andes · Bogotá, Colombia
01 The problem

Ore hauling: the cycle that moves the mine, and its budget

Loaders at the pit face fill haul trucks that carry blasted rock to unloading points and return for the next load, until the shift's production target is met.

1

Which loader serves each truck?

assignment

Loading time depends on the pair: a CAT 777G takes 3 min on the excavator and 4 min on the wheel loader. The fast loader is a scarce resource.

2

When does each trip start?

sequencing · release times

A loader serves one truck at a time and a truck can only reload once it is back from its previous trip. Queues at the loader are pure waste.

3

Where does each trip unload?

routing

Three unloading points at different distances: u₂ costs one extra minute of hauling, and each point admits at most Cu trucks at once.

4

How many trips until the target?

production goal

The number of trips is not given in advance: trips are scheduled until the hauled volume reaches G. Bigger trucks need fewer trips but load more slowly.

★

Finish the target as early as possible

objective · makespan

The quality of a shift plan is the time at which the last trip that completes the target is finished: the makespan Cmax. Minimizing it releases the fleet for the next block.

50–60 %
of the operating cost of the extraction cycle is hauling (Alarie & Gamache, 2002)
2 · 2 · 3
loader models, truck models and unloading points in the real case: a ferronickel open-pit mine in Colombia
3 → 17
trucks in the operational fleets we schedule; exact methods stop scaling in this range

From the pit to a parallel-machine scheduling problem

Loading equipmentexcavator CAT 9926 · wheel loader CAT 990H
→
Machines Muniform parallel machines: each loader has its own speed
One haul-truck tripload · haul · unload · return
→
Joba truck performs a sequence of jobs during the shift
Loading time pmvdepends on the loader and the truck model
→
Machine-dependent processing time3 / 4 min for a 777G, 2 / 3 min for a 773D
Haul, unload and return rvu3–4 min for a 777G, 2–3 min for a 773D
→
Release time rjthe truck's next job cannot start before it is back
Unloading points U with capacity Cuthree destinations at different distances
→
Routing decision + resource limitat most Cu trucks in transit to u at a time
Production target G = 1000 m³60 m³ or 34 m³ per trip
→
Open job setschedule trips until Σ qv ≥ G
Time to complete the targetthe shift plan's quality
→
Objective: minimize the makespan Cmaxcompletion time of the last trip
Qm| rj| Cmax
NP-hard
Even two identical loaders with no release times (P2 || Cmax) already make the problem NP-hard (Graham et al., 1979). Qm | rj | Cmax inherits it: exact methods stop scaling at 10–20 trucks, exactly the size of an operational fleet.

03 Related work

Twenty-four studies, four dimensions, none of them together

dimension i

Heterogeneous loaders qm

Loaders with different speeds, so the same truck takes a different time on each machine.

  • Paricheh & Osanloo (2019)
  • Abolghasemian et al. (2020)
  • Tarazona-Torres et al. (2024)
  • field studies: Yupanqui; Gutierrez Torres; Pauca Mantilla (2019)
Commonmodelled in most formal MIPs
dimension ii

Release times ri

Truck travel time as the moment a truck becomes available again at the loader.

  • Martinez (2019)
  • Tomás & León (2020)
  • Salgado Gaspar (2020)
  • Both & Dimitrakopoulos (2020)
  • Mohtasham et al. (2021)
Frequentmostly in queueing and field studies
dimension iii

Unloading points |U| > 2

Several destinations with their own distance and capacity, so routing becomes part of the schedule.

  • most studies: ≤ 2 loaders and ≤ 2 unloading points
  • few exceptions, e.g. Mohtasham et al. (2021)
Rarerouting usually fixed a priori
dimension iv

Exact vs. approximate, same framework

Exact models and heuristics compared head-to-head on the same instances.

  • exact: Paricheh & Osanloo; De la Cruz Ortiz; Bakhtavar et al.; Mohtasham et al.; Upadhyay et al.
  • approximate: Yupanqui; Abolghasemian et al.; Kuckartz et al.; Mnzool et al.; Das et al. (IP + SA)
Splitone family or the other, rarely both
This studyMFOHOSM framework
✓ two loader models with different speeds
✓ truck return as release time
✓ |U| = 3 unloading points with capacity
✓ exact model + 5 approximate strategies on 15 shared instances

Closest predecessors: Tarazona-Torres et al. (2024, Algorithms) covered (i) and (ii) with a time-and-cost MIP; Paipilla & Pulido (2024) extended it with fleet sizing. This work adds the unloading-point dimension and formal metaheuristics compared against the exact model.

04 Solution approach

Five strategies, one benchmark, one framework

Optimization strategiesall evaluated on the same 15 instances, hardware and metric (makespan gap to the exact model)
Exactoptimality certificate, high cost
mixed-integer programming

MFOHOSM

Time-indexed MIP with binary start, busy and in-transit variables and a continuous makespan. Solved with Gurobi 10.0.1.

stop: 3 h time limit
Approximatefast, no certificate
constructive

FIFO

Trucks in fleet order, loaders rotate round-robin after each pass, nearest unloading point. The rule most simulators use.

≈ 0 s
constructive

SPT

Trucks ordered by shortest loading time; picks the (loader, unloading point) pair that ends the cycle earliest, with a queue at each point.

≈ 0 s
local search

INSERT

From FIFO, reassign one trip's loader or unloading point, re-time the sequence, move to the best of a random sample of neighbours.

K = 1000 · η = 50
tabu search

TSI

Starts from INSERT's best. Full INSERT neighbourhood, tabu list against cycling, aspiration criterion, perturbation when the search stalls.

τ = 5 · σlim = 20 · K = 1000
tabu search

TSI-S

TSI plus SWAP moves that exchange two trips in the sequence; sampled neighbourhood and a stronger perturbation (loader and unloading point).

τ = 5 · σlim = 20 · η = 50
shared encoding every approximate strategy handles an ordered list of trips 𝒜 = [(v, m, u), …] and a RECALCULATE routine that re-times it
assumptions (i) refuelling and waiting times negligible   (ii) equipment always available   (iii) several unloading points

12 Results · statistics

Are the differences real? Paired tests over the fifteen instances

step 1

Shapiro–Wilk

Paired differences Cmax(strategy) − Cmax(MFOHOSM) are not normal: p < 0.05 for all five strategies.
→
step 2

Non-parametric route

The paired t-test is ruled out; the Wilcoxon signed-rank test compares each strategy with the exact model instance by instance.
→
step 3

Wilcoxon vs. MFOHOSM

Every paired difference is ≥ 0, so the negative rank sum is zero: all five strategies differ significantly from the exact model (p = 0.001).

Each strategy against MFOHOSM (n = 15 paired instances)

Z is the same for all strategies because the exact model wins on every instance; this test says that they differ, not how much. The ranking question needs a test among the approximate strategies themselves.

Friedman test among the five approximate strategies

χ² = 12.35 · df = 4 · p = 0.015

Blocks = instances, treatments = strategies, response = Cmax. The null hypothesis of equal performance is rejected; Kendall's W = 0.21 (moderate agreement across instances). Mean rank, 1 = best:

Post-hoc: TSI against each other strategy (exact Wilcoxon, two-sided, Holm-adjusted)

TSI has the best mean rank and is never worse than INSERT except once; against SPT the evidence is inconclusive on 15 instances, although SPT's gap doubles on the largest fleets.

13 Conclusions

A clear trade-off, and a practical way through it

1

The formulation fits the operation

Loaders as uniform parallel machines, truck returns as release times, three unloading points and an open number of trips: Qm | rj | Cmax captures the shift plan without a simulator.

2

The exact model is the benchmark, not the tool

MFOHOSM reaches a 1.97 % optimality gap on average but needs two hours per instance and hits the time limit on mid-size fleets.

3

TSI is the operational alternative

Best mean rank among the approximate strategies, 9.5 % average gap in about 90 s, two orders of magnitude faster than the exact model, and within 1.5–6 % on the largest fleets.

4

Memory matters more than neighbourhood size

TSI beats plain INSERT on 11 of 15 instances (Holm p = 0.02); adding SWAP moves (TSI-S) ties on 9 instances and costs 13× the time.

Future work

  • Tighten TSI without paying in time: better initial solutions, candidate lists, adaptive tenure.
  • Uncertainty: stochastic loading and cycle times, equipment breakdowns and refuelling, which the experiments assumed away.
  • Rolling horizon: multi-shift plans with dynamic release times and re-optimization as trucks report back.
  • Stronger exact bounds: a compact or time-bucket reformulation of MFOHOSM to certify the metaheuristics on large fleets.

Simplifying assumptions in this study: permanent equipment availability and deterministic service times.
